newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone coupmakers defy Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coupmakers defy Nigeria.

text.p: Sierra Leone coup leaders told Nigeria on Thursday they would not restore the ousted civilian government of Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, saying this would jeopardise a new-found peace between the army and rebels.

Sierra Leone's chief of defence staff Brigadier Samuel Koroma said they had been unable to reach any agreement with a delegation sent by Nigerian military leader General Sani Abacha which arrived on Wednesday.

"We are not prepared to hand over to former president Kabbah. If president Kabbah takes over again, he will jeopardise the peace that we have been able to achieve with the RUF rebels," he told reporters.

Foday Sankoh's Revolutionary United Front has been fighting a bush war since 1991. A peace accord signed with Kabbah last November failed to hold, and the rebels have joined forces with the coup soldiers.
Coup leader Major Johnny Paul Koromah named Sankoh vice-chairman in his Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC).

"We have sent a message to the Nigerian head of state through the Nigerian delegation which arrived yesterday in Freetown, saying that General Abacha must choose between peace in Sierra Leone or the forced return of President Kabbah to power by Nigeria and ECOMOG," Koroma said.
Nigeria, which already had troops of the West African ECOMOG force in Freetown under a defence agreement, has been steadily reinforcing in the city since the May 25 coup.
Nigerian gunboats shelled the capital on Monday in a show of force. Rebels responded by attacking Nigerian troops guarding foreigners at a hotel.

Koroma said if Nigerian-led forces restored Kabbah to power the military would overthrow him again, but he promised the AFRC would organise elections within 18 months to two years "for the people to choose the leader they want".
Koroma said a Ghanaian delegation reported heading for Freetown had not yet arrived.
Witnesses said the Sierra Leone army had cleared out a large colonial-era bunker above the city by Fourah Bay College on Mount Aureol. Students had fled the college fearing an attack.
Canadian miner DiamondWorks said it had temporarily evacuated its mining personnel from the eastern town of Koidu and suspended its bulk diamond sampling operations.
It said its South African trained security team would remain at the Koidu mine "to protect DiamondWorks' assets".

The impoverished, war-torn country's third coup in five years has been condemned at home and abroad. The Organisation of African Unity summit, which ended in Harare on Wednesday, called for restoration of Kabbah, who was elected in March 1996 after four years of army rule. He is now in neighbouring Guinea.
Many Freetown residents have refused to go to work since the coup as a sign of protest. Some shops are open but food and fuel are in short supply.
Thousands of people have fled the capital for the provinces. Residents have virtually abandoned the seafront Aberdeen district, which was hit by shells on Monday.
The military say 80 people were killed on Monday, other sources put the number at less than 50.

Most evacuees have been brought initially to the Guinean capital Conakry. Britain chartered a Boeing 747 to bring evacuees to London on Thursday, and a Middle East Airlines plane flew 500 Lebanese to Beirut.
